title: Superconductivity of Tellurium Polyhydride with Tc above 90K
authors: Jinfu Zhu, Guiqi Liu, Yuanhao Su, Hongyu Liu, Sijia Zhang, Panpan Kong, Qingqing Liu, Jianfa Zhao, Shaomin Feng, Jun Zhang, Haoyu Zheng, Jing Song, Luhong Wang, Fuyang Liu, Haozhe Liu, M. Bykov, Xiancheng Wang, Changqing Jin
abstract: We report experimental diacovery of superconductivity (SC) in tellurium (Te) polyhydride. The compound was synthesized at high pressure and high temperature conditions using a diamond anvil cell combined with a laser heating system. Subsequent in situ transport measurements at high pressures, performed as a function of temperature and applied magnetic field, revealed a superconducting transition with a critical temperature Tc about 91 K at 263 GPa. The superconducting phase is assigned to TeH4 with characterized face shared TeH12 cage forming quasi molecular H2 units based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction experiments. Analysis of the SC behavior at magnetic fields yielded a Ginzburg Landau (GL) coherence length of approximately 47 angstroms. Tellurium polyhydride thus becomes another chalcogen polyhydride superconductor in addition to the landmark discovery of the first polyhydride high Tc SC SH3.
summary: This work reports the discovery of superconductivity in tellurium polyhydride ($	ext{TeH}_4$) at high pressures, achieving a critical temperature of about 91 K. Using *in situ* transport and XRD measurements, the authors characterized the superconducting phase and determined key parameters like the coherence length. This adds to the growing body of knowledge regarding high-temperature superconductivity in hydrides.
main_problem: The paper reports the experimental discovery of superconductivity in tellurium (Te) polyhydride under extreme high pressure.
main_result: Superconductivity was observed in the $	ext{TeH}_4$ phase with a critical temperature ($T_c$) of approximately 91 K at 263 GPa, establishing it as a new chalcogen polyhydride superconductor.
method: The study employed *in situ* transport measurements (resistance vs. T and B) and high-pressure X-ray diffraction (XRD) within a diamond anvil cell.
model_or_system: The physical system is tellurium polyhydride ($	ext{TeH}_x$), specifically identifying the superconducting phase as $	ext{TeH}_4$. The structure is characterized by face-sharing $	ext{TeH}_{12}$ cages forming quasi-molecular $	ext{H}_2$ units.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), zero resistance state, upper critical magnetic field ($\mu_0H_{c2}(T)$), and Ginzburg-Landau coherence length ($\xi$).
important_parameters: High pressures (up to 263 GPa), high temperatures, and applied magnetic fields (up to 5 T).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting $\mu_0H_{c2}(T)$ data to WHH and GL theories, and the superconducting phase is assigned to the hexagonal $	ext{TeH}_4$ structure.
figures_summary: Figures detail the temperature and magnetic field dependence of resistance ($R(T)$) showing the superconducting transition, and plots of $\mu_0H_{c2}(T)$ derived from these measurements.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of reporting the experimental setup (DAC, *in situ* measurements), presenting the structural characterization (XRD confirming $	ext{TeH}_4$), and then detailing the transport measurements to confirm the superconducting transition and analyze its parameters ($T_c$, $\mu_0H_{c2}$, $\xi$).
why_interesting: While focused on high-pressure solid-state physics, the study's rigorous measurement of superconducting parameters ($T_c$, $\mu_0H_{c2}$) and structural confirmation under extreme conditions provides valuable data points for understanding unconventional pairing mechanisms in correlated materials.
